metadata.title: ETF Zoo: How the Election Splits Big Tech

content.text:
In an episode recorded the day after elections, ETF Zoo hosts Dave Nadig, ETF.com's President & Director of Research, and Sumit Roy, Senior Analyst at ETF.com, were joined by Aniket Ullal, Head, ETF Research and Analytics at CFRA Research, and Jeffrey Ptak, Managing Director of Morningstar to talk post-election tech bifurcation and more. The S&P 500 closed up nearly 2% on Wednesday, but the gain hid large moves underneath, with some healthcare stocks jumping 20% while data center names fell as much as 15%. Roy pointed to a sharp split within tech as hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Google rose 5% to 7%, while semiconductor makers such as NVIDIA, Broadcom and Intel fell. They're trends that continued into trading Friday. The thinking is based on the potential slowing of the data center buildout that would cut chip demand but make existing data centers more valuable to the companies that already own the most of them.
The Zoo crew also dug into how AI-related debt is spreading through fixed income. There's an argument to be made that the wave of AI-linked issuance in corporate bond ETFs actually helps bond investors by diversifying portfolios that lean heavily toward utilities and financials, and it offers investment-grade exposure at higher yields. The catch is that investors may end up exposed twice when they also own the same companies' stock. However, everyone was skeptical about the latest attempts at credit default swap ETFs.
On asset allocation, bond investors finally appear to be paid for duration risk. Higher yields and shorter durations have improved the risk-reward balance in intermediate Treasuries. Much of the recent risk-off flow has gone into a single fund, Schwab's dividend ETF, up more than 30% this year and now the largest dividend ETF in the U.S., which suggests performance chasing. Ptak also shared research showing that active is a spectrum rather than a yes-or-no label and how discretionary active managers beat their benchmarks less often over the past decade than pure index trackers did. Meanwhile, systematic active shops like Dimensional and Avantis posted strong beat rates.
The episode closed on how far the ETF wrapper keeps stretching. Ptak's updated study of 2x single-stock ETFs found that issuers pick strong underlying stocks but volatility decay, fees and financing costs erode the benefit of leverage over longer holding periods. That said, these products aren't going away due to their ongoing popularity with short-term traders. On uncapped sector ETFs, the panel was divided. Roy saw value in getting true sector weights while Ullal countered that funds made up largely of Meta and Google, or nearly half Amazon, are close to owning the stock outright. The group also questioned the 56 newly filed long-call "Power Max" ETFs, since retail traders can already buy options directly. Ptak offered one possible use case: leverage over a longer period than daily-reset products allow. The debut of single-stock perpetual futures on Kalshi could also create future competition for leveraged ETFs.
